item.title: Videostrong Built a Backdoor Into 1.3 Million Android TV Boxes and Sold the Access to Criminals
item.description:
1,472,554 TV boxes and other Android devices in over 170 countries shipped with a backdoor. The owners did nothing wrong. The maker put it in the firmware, at least since 2020, and sold access to criminals.

On November 2, Google’s threat intelligence team named the company behind the backdoor: Videostrong Technology, a manufacturer in China that designs and builds Android TV boxes for its own brands and for other companies. The team writes with high confidence that Videostrong developed the backdoor, put it on its boxes, turned them into a botnet and ran it for profit, as a deliberate campaign by the company itself. The team calls a device maker that infects its own users on purpose an unacceptable breach of trust. Videostrong then sold access to those boxes to other criminal groups, who paid to load their own software onto them.

The count of 1,472,554 comes from TrendAI, which measured the operation between June and October 2026 and found the backdoor in 206 different models of TV boxes, projectors and other Android devices. Its collection had gaps, so the researchers call that number a lower limit. Most of the devices are in Malaysia, Brazil, Iraq, Mexico and Taiwan. In the United States, Germany, the United Kingdom, Australia and Canada, the count lies between about 26,000 and 42,000 devices per country. Over those four months, 3,849,226 different home and mobile IP addresses showed up as exit points for internet traffic that other people paid to send through these boxes. A second research team puts the number of devices that contact the operators’ servers on any given day at around half a million.

One of the boxes is the MECOOL KM9PRO Max. Its maker announced it on December 5, 2024, as a 4K streaming box certified by Google and Netflix, and pitched it as a Christmas present. At IFA in Berlin in 2025, Videostrong presented itself as a maker of Google certified and Dolby approved devices. That second research team is Synthient, a company that tracks proxy networks, and its researchers bought a KM9PRO Max in late 2025. They switched on developer mode and connected to it over ADB, the Android Debug Bridge that developers use to control an Android device from a computer, on port 5555. Then they dumped the apps and processes that were running. The backdoor was already there, running with system rights under the name com.oemservice.

Before a box may ship with the Play Store on it, its software has to pass a set of compatibility and security tests. Videostrong scrambled its code so the tests could not see what it did, a trick called obfuscation, and the malicious part only loaded after the buyer switched the box on for the first time. The threat intelligence team writes that Videostrong exploited a gap in those tests, and that the review process has been changed because of it.

The backdoor itself is called x.cpe, and in some builds it runs as com.oemservice. It starts as a small starter program, called a stub, in the system part of the firmware, with the same rights as Android’s own system processes, the level Android calls android.uid.system. When the box boots, the stub looks in a separate partition called /oem/ for the full package and installs it into /data/app/. An owner who finds it there and uninstalls it gets it back at the next restart. As a normal user, there is no way to get rid of it.

When the box starts, it sends its device information to a server under anyevonline[.]com. The server answers with login details for a second server that uses MQTT, a small messaging protocol. From that moment the box keeps a connection open to mqtt.szbboys[.]com on ports 3885, 3886 and 3887, and waits for orders. Each check-in message it sends contains information about the device, and also the e-mail address of the user, if someone is signed in on the box.

Before it installs anything, the backdoor wipes the setting on the box that records what the user agreed to. Then it turns off Play Protect, the scanner that checks apps on Android devices. From there it can install apps without asking, run shell commands and scripts, take screenshots of what is on the TV, send key presses to the box and map the network it sits on with ping and traceroute tests. In the four months of counting, silent install commands reached more than 187,000 devices, and the operators could also collect Wi-Fi and Bluetooth data from the boxes.

The money came from what Videostrong let other companies run on the boxes, and the largest part was proxy software. About 1.33 million of the counted devices were lined up to get that extra software, the proxy and ad fraud modules. A residential proxy sells access to home internet connections. A customer pays, and their traffic goes out onto the internet from a living room, with that household’s IP address on it, while the household has no idea.

The threat intelligence report lists modules from Honeygain and NetNut among the proxy providers, plus six more. Next to the proxies came ad fraud modules that load ads in the background and click on them. Four more backdoors came along as well, among them Moyu and Bird, which researchers had seen before in BadBox, an earlier operation built on backdoored TV boxes. The groups behind those modules also had other ways onto devices, and their servers reach at least 10 million more compromised devices on top of the 1.3 million, according to the same report.

Besides TV boxes, x.cpe also turned up on telehealth devices, karaoke machines and digital signs.

The oldest x.cpe sample in the researchers’ published list was first seen on December 14, 2020, as version 3.6.5. In late 2024, Videostrong moved the modules that made the money out of x.cpe and into a separate app called com.abc.nexus, possibly in response to earlier enforcement against those older backdoored boxes. Nexus bundled several proxy programs into one app, and the researchers traced it through a series of versions, with proxy providers added and removed along the way.

In August 2026 the operators changed course again, and Nexus was uninstalled from boxes across the botnet. New packages arrived through the messaging connection, named to look like part of Android: com.android.system.ntp and com.android.sso.auth.handler. Several versions of them unpack a file called libexploit.so. That file restarts adbd, the service behind ADB, with root rights and opens a shell through it. The package then uses that shell to copy itself into /system/priv-app/, and writes a permissions file that lets it install packages and reboot the box. Some of the payloads came from a public code repository called Aviciiii/ott, filled with device images and backdoors, which now returns a 404.

The trail to Videostrong runs through Kimwolf, the botnet I wrote about in January, which reached at least 2 million devices, mostly Android TV boxes with an open debug port, through a hole in a proxy service. While tracking that botnet, the same researchers saw boxes of this kind getting infected, and MECOOL devices were among them. Boxes like these are popular for pirated streams, and together with the Motion Picture Association, the film industry group that fights piracy, the researchers bought several of them to take apart.

Following the servers, the researchers found that the command server anyevonline[.]com has a subdomain, file.anyevonline[.]com on port 8000, with an open directory that was reachable from the internet without a login. Inside were the backdoors the operators used, and a folder named pdf. In that folder was a signed device declaration from Owen Cao, the R&D director of Videostrong. The domain videostrong.cn points to the same IP address as mqtt.anyevonline[.]com, the operators’ admin panel, where they could see their victims and hand out tasks.

The operators signed the backdoors with Videostrong e-mail addresses. In the list of traces the researchers published, the certificate for the over-the-air updates and the certificate that signs the Yoka apps and the CPE app itself both carry the same address, hong.luo@videostrong.com. The threat intelligence report also lists eleven accounts on a code-hosting site that served the operators’ packages, and one of them is called yf-videostrong.

The message server is called szbboys, and Bboys also shows up in the trademark records of the United States Patent and Trademark Office. There, the MECOOL trademark belongs to Shenzhen Bboys Technology Co., Ltd., on the 5th floor of the Lushi Industry Building in the Bao’an 28 District. The same company holds the US trademarks YOKATV and M8S PLUS.

YOKATV used to belong to Videostrong itself, which registered it in 2016. That registration lapsed, and the office cancelled it on August 4, 2023. On November 25, 2023, the MECOOL trademark holder filed for the same name and got it registered in October 2024. Yokatv.com is one of the storefronts where the researchers found the backdoored devices for sale, and M8S_PLUS is one of the model names on their list. Videostrong’s own website gives its address as the 6th floor of the Lushi Industrial East Building, in that same district.

That website now leads with AI companion robots and products for elderly care. The company sells the HC1 Home Care Hub for elderly care and telehealth, with a 1080p camera and two microphones, and it supports MQTT, the same protocol the backdoor uses. Its KA1 is a smart speaker with an Android TV box inside, and its KA2 is a box with a full HD camera, a microphone array, a speaker and Android TV. MECOOL’s own store sells them as the HomePlus KA1 and the Now KA2, the second one as Google certified video calling on TV.

All three model names appear on the list of 182 model names seen in this campaign. The researchers add that a model name on its own does not prove a device is infected, and nothing on that list shows these are the same products. The HC1 product page says Videostrong does not store or share voice, image or video data from its devices.

Last week, Google took the operation down together with Japan’s National Police Agency and five security companies, among them the two research teams named here. Through legal action, it took down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the boxes and push its modules, along with the command servers of more than a dozen malware families the backdoor loaded onto them. It also cut its ties with Videostrong and banned the company, and any future subsidiary or affiliate, from building certified Android devices or supplying software to other certified makers. Videostrong did not immediately respond to questions from The Register.

The servers are gone, but the backdoor is still on the boxes. It sits in the firmware and puts itself back after a restart, and the owner cannot remove it. The team that counted the boxes says cleaning them needs the vendor or the platform to act, or a new device. The advice from the team that bought the box is shorter: get rid of it, because it may still carry other malware.

The threat intelligence team also points at the shops. Retailers and online marketplaces that sell these boxes share responsibility, it writes, and should demand independent security audits from manufacturers and quickly stop selling devices from the makers caught doing this. The researchers who bought the box go further and want these devices pulled from online stores and marketplaces right away.

To see which box you have, open the settings and look up the model name, then compare it with the list of 182 model names in Synthient’s public research repository on GitHub. With network debugging switched on in the box’s developer options, a computer on the same network can check for the package names from the report:

1
2
3
4
5
6

adb connect 192.168.1.50:5555
adb shell pm list packages oemservice
adb shell pm list packages cpe
adb shell pm list packages abc.nexus
adb shell pm list packages system.ntp
adb shell pm list packages sso.auth

Replace 192.168.1.50 with the IP address of the box. A line that starts with package: means the name is installed. Take a box that shows one of them off the network. Switch network debugging off again when you are done, because an open debugging port on the home network is how the botnet from January got onto boxes like these.

The report gives owners this advice:

  • → Keep the built-in app scanner turned on
  • → Stay away from apps that pay for unused bandwidth or for sharing your internet connection
  • → Buy boxes from brands on the Android TV partner list

On these boxes the first tip does not help, because the backdoor itself sets package_verifier_user_consent to -1, and that switches the scanner off. The box from the start of this story was advertised as Google certified.

Which devices on your own network answer on port 5555, and which one keeps talking to the internet while the TV is switched off?

item.title: mSecure Password Manager Tells Customers to Replace Their Passwords, 2FA and Passkeys Without Saying Why
item.description:
Customers with close to 1,000 logins in one password manager got one email: change the passwords, reset the 2FA, remove the passkeys. No reason given. A German government test flagged it 11 months earlier.

After a few years, almost everything ends up in your password manager. The login for your bank, your email, your work accounts, the six-digit codes for two-factor login, and lately your passkeys as well. You remember one master password, and the app remembers the rest.

On November 3, customers of the password manager mSecure opened an email from mSeven Software, the company in Lake Oswego, Oregon, that makes the app. Former customers, who had stopped using it, got the same email.

It said the company had “recently learned of suspicious activity” connected to mSecure. They had started an investigation, taken steps to limit the damage, and brought in outside security experts. Then came the advice. Because of the potential security implications, you should immediately protect the confidential information you keep in the app. That could mean changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication, or removing existing passkeys.

This week they did warn them, without saying what happened, and told them to replace almost everything.

  • → After that, your bank, your work accounts, and any password you used on more than one site

item.title: Scamwich Fake Restaurant Ordering Sites
item.description:
820 fake ordering sites for 35 restaurant chains showed the restaurant’s own menu, then took the card and the bank’s text code. The customers did nothing wrong. Google ran the ads from July to October.

Someone wants lunch from Jimmy John’s. They type the name into Google instead of typing the web address, and at the top of the results sits a listing that looks like the restaurant’s own. The headline says something like Order Sandwiches for Pick Up, with a line about delivery, catering or a location near you. One click, and an ordering page opens with the sandwiches and the opening hours, and the prices match the restaurant’s.

They match because the fake site borrows them. Each time you click, it quietly asks the restaurant’s website for that same page, gets it back, puts its own web address where the restaurant’s was, and shows it to you. You are looking at the restaurant’s own page, passed through somebody else’s server. That setup is called a reverse proxy.

The scam runs on it.

So when the restaurant changes a price at noon, the fake site shows the new price at noon too. Even the restaurant’s own bot check keeps running on the page, because the fake site fixes its links so it still works. The researchers who found the network, at a company called InfoHawk, named it Scamwich and say the restaurant itself never had to be hacked.

Only one part of the page gets swapped. At checkout, the box where you type your card normally comes from the company that handles the restaurant’s payments. The fake site puts its own box there instead. A little script keeps an eye on the page, and if the original box comes back, it swaps that box out again.

A second script looks at the Place order button twice a second and copies the total. So the fake box shows the exact amount in your cart, down to the cent.

The address bar does not help you either. The sites sit behind Cloudflare, a service that hides where a website actually runs and gives it the file your browser checks before it calls a connection secure. That file is called a certificate, and these sites had valid ones. In the example the researchers show, the certificate came from Google Trust Services.

So the browser tells you the connection is secure. That only means outsiders cannot read what travels between you and the site. The site itself belonged to the scammers.

The fake box asks for the card number, the expiry date, the three digits on the back, your name and your phone number. The moment you press pay, those details go to the scammer, along with the name of the fake site.

The details arrive right away, over a connection between your browser and their server that stays open while you are on the page. The tool behind that is called socket.io. Someone on the other side can see your card as soon as you send it.

What happens next is what the researchers think this kit, the fake pages and scripts behind each site, was made for. A person sits behind a control panel and uses your card somewhere else.

Many banks ask for one more check when you pay online: a code by text message, or a tap to approve in your banking app. That way a card number alone is not enough. The check is called 3-D Secure. Here, it works against you.

Because when your bank sends that code, the scammer pushes a new page onto your screen. One page says the card was declined and asks for another. One asks for the code that came in on your phone. One asks you to approve the payment in your banking app. One says the code was wrong and asks you to type it again.

You type the code to pay for your lunch. According to the researchers, that code is what lets the scammer’s own purchase through the bank’s check. That is their reading of the kit; the report does not show a payment going through.

When the scammer is done, the page drops a small file in your browser, a cookie named valid with the value 77777, set to last until 2038. In the copy the researchers took apart, it then sends you on to the website of another chain, Jimmy John’s, through a link service called href.li that hides where you came from.

No order ever reaches the restaurant. You wait for food that is not coming, and according to the researchers your card has paid for whatever the scammer bought.

The researchers counted 820 of these fake web addresses across two rounds of searching, copies of 35 restaurant chains. 808 of them end in .delivery. That is the last part of a web address, like .com, and this one is official, added to the internet’s address system in 2014 and run by a company called Identity Digital. For a site where you order food, it sounds exactly right. The rest end in .com or .shop.

Jimmy John’s alone had 404 fake domains. Firehouse Subs had 121, with names like flrehousesubs.delivery, an l where the i should be. Jersey Mike’s had 80, among them mlckessejersstey.delivery and jerseymikes-delivery.com. Dave’s Hot Chicken had 67.

Waffle House got w0ffleh0use.delivery, with zeros for the a and the o. Chipotle, Popeyes, Panera Bread, Five Guys, Little Caesars, Tim Hortons and Wawa are on the list as well, some with a single copy, some with a handful. The earliest copy in the research turned up on March 3, 2026.

Almost all of them, 761 of the 820, sit behind that same service that hides their servers. Of the first 255 the researchers found, 251 were bought from the same shop for web addresses, Dynadot. A shop like that is called a registrar.

One server had a live card panel on it, the place where the card details arrive. A second group of 68 domains is tied to a server on Amazon’s cloud, and some of those sites run straight from it, in Frankfurt, with a slightly different script. The researchers found nothing that shows the same people run both.

In cybersecurity, attribution is one of the hardest problems. A kit can be shared or sold. A server address tells you where a machine is rented, not who rents it. What we know for sure is how these sites work.

On November 4, 367 of the 820 domains still served a site.

To bring people to them, the scammers bought Google search ads. The researchers found at least 47 of them between July 7 and October 20, 2026. And they only looked up ads for the sites from their first search, so there were probably more.

The ads ran under 46 separate advertiser accounts with 43 different business names, and those names look unrelated to the chains: construction firms, a watch company, a reptile rescue. How the scammers got hold of those accounts, the researchers do not say. Most ads ran for one to four days, usually starting a few days after the domain was registered. The longest ran for 56 days, the next for 39.

Google publishes a report each year about the bad ads it stops. The one for 2025 came out on April 16, 2026. The company says it blocked or removed more than 8.3 billion ads and shut down 24.9 million accounts. Its systems caught over 99 percent of the ads that broke its rules before they were ever shown, the report says, and 602 million ads had to do with scams. It also says it checks who its advertisers are.

These 47 got through. Some stayed up for weeks.

An advertiser can pay Google to show an ad when someone searches for another company’s name. That search word is called a keyword, and Google’s trademark policy does not restrict using someone else’s brand there. Many of the ads also put the brand name in the headline itself, followed by words like Menu Items or Catering Menu.

The 20 Jimmy John’s ads did not. Their headlines said Sandwich Shop or Order Sandwiches for Delivery, so a trademark complaint from the chain would have found no brand name in the ad to point at.

Google has a second rule that needs no complaint at all. Its policy against misleading ads bans pretending to be another brand or business, in the ad or on the website behind it. It treats that as one of its most serious violations and can suspend the account without warning. These ads sent people to sites that pretended to be the restaurant. They still ran, most of them for a few days only.

The man whose company found all of this knows the ad business from the inside. Rob Leathern, its CEO and co-founder, was VP of Privacy and Security Product at Google and led Business Integrity at Meta, according to its own team page. The company sells tools to detect exactly this kind of clone, and the report ends with an offer to check whether someone is copying your brand.

The trick itself is older than this campaign. On February 24, 2023, the writer Cory Doctorow described searching for a Thai restaurant he liked in Burbank, Kiin Thai. He clicked a sponsored result for a site called kiinthaila.com, built on Wix, while the restaurant’s own website was the third link down. The copy added 15 percent to the prices, passed the order on to the restaurant and billed him twice.

The restaurant called him to cancel and told him to contact his card company to get the charge reversed. That version still produced an order. The 2026 version produces none, shows the restaurant’s live menu instead of a copied one, and goes after your bank code too.

Two months before that post, on December 21, 2022, the FBI had already warned about this. It wrote that criminals were buying search ads with web addresses that look like a known business. Those ads showed up at the very top of the results and looked almost the same as the normal ones. Its advice back then: check the address before you click an ad, type the address of a business yourself instead of searching for it, and use an ad blocker.

The chains in this campaign are American. A fake site that pulls the pages from the original and only swaps the payment box would work the same way for a pizza place in Rotterdam or a delivery service in Berlin.

By November 3, none of the ads the researchers found were still running, and Google’s own page for looking up ads now shows Can’t find ad for them.

Restaurants have one way to spot this early. The fake site has to ask the restaurant’s own server for each page. So a chain that watches for its pages showing up under a strange web address, or for checkouts that never reach its payment company, can catch these sites fast.

What you can do before you pay for food online:

  • → Type the restaurant’s address yourself, use a bookmark, or order through its own app
  • → Look at the domain in the address bar. A secure connection only tells you it is encrypted
  • → A brand name followed by .delivery, -delivery.com or -us.com was the pattern in this campaign
  • → Read the full text from your bank before you type a code anywhere. If the shop or the amount does not match your order, stop
  • → Pay with a credit card where you can, so you can dispute the charge
  • → Use an ad blocker, one of the tips from that 2022 warning
  • → If you typed your card into a site like this, call your bank, block the card, and in the US report it at ic3.gov

Want to see what a server in the middle can read? Run Burp Suite in your own lab and watch your browser’s traffic pass through. Someone wants lunch from Jimmy John’s. They type the name into Google instead of typing the web address, and at the top of the results sits a listing that looks like the restaurant’s own. The headline says something like Order Sandwiches for Pick Up, with a line about delivery, catering or a location near you. One click, and an ordering page opens with the sandwiches and the opening hours, and the prices match the restaurant’s.

They match because the fake site borrows them. Each time you click, it quietly asks the restaurant’s website for that same page, gets it back, puts its own web address where the restaurant’s was, and shows it to you. You are looking at the restaurant’s own page, passed through somebody else’s server. That setup is called a reverse proxy.

The scam runs on it.

So when the restaurant changes a price at noon, the fake site shows the new price at noon too. Even the restaurant’s own bot check keeps running on the page, because the fake site fixes its links so it still works. The researchers who found the network, at a company called InfoHawk, named it Scamwich and say the restaurant itself never had to be hacked.

Only one part of the page gets swapped. At checkout, the box where you type your card normally comes from the company that handles the restaurant’s payments. The fake site puts its own box there instead. A little script keeps an eye on the page, and if the original box comes back, it swaps that box out again.

A second script looks at the Place order button twice a second and copies the total. So the fake box shows the exact amount in your cart, down to the cent.

The address bar does not help you either. The sites sit behind Cloudflare, a service that hides where a website actually runs and gives it the file your browser checks before it calls a connection secure. That file is called a certificate, and these sites had valid ones. In the example the researchers show, the certificate came from Google Trust Services.

So the browser tells you the connection is secure. That only means outsiders cannot read what travels between you and the site. The site itself belonged to the scammers.

The fake box asks for the card number, the expiry date, the three digits on the back, your name and your phone number. The moment you press pay, those details go to the scammer, along with the name of the fake site.

The details arrive right away, over a connection between your browser and their server that stays open while you are on the page. The tool behind that is called socket.io. Someone on the other side can see your card as soon as you send it.

What happens next is what the researchers think this kit, the fake pages and scripts behind each site, was made for. A person sits behind a control panel and uses your card somewhere else.

Many banks ask for one more check when you pay online: a code by text message, or a tap to approve in your banking app. That way a card number alone is not enough. The check is called 3-D Secure. Here, it works against you.

Because when your bank sends that code, the scammer pushes a new page onto your screen. One page says the card was declined and asks for another. One asks for the code that came in on your phone. One asks you to approve the payment in your banking app. One says the code was wrong and asks you to type it again.

You type the code to pay for your lunch. According to the researchers, that code is what lets the scammer’s own purchase through the bank’s check. That is their reading of the kit; the report does not show a payment going through.

When the scammer is done, the page drops a small file in your browser, a cookie named valid with the value 77777, set to last until 2038. In the copy the researchers took apart, it then sends you on to the website of another chain, Jimmy John’s, through a link service called href.li that hides where you came from.

No order ever reaches the restaurant. You wait for food that is not coming, and according to the researchers your card has paid for whatever the scammer bought.

The researchers counted 820 of these fake web addresses across two rounds of searching, copies of 35 restaurant chains. 808 of them end in .delivery. That is the last part of a web address, like .com, and this one is official, added to the internet’s address system in 2014 and run by a company called Identity Digital. For a site where you order food, it sounds exactly right. The rest end in .com or .shop.

Jimmy John’s alone had 404 fake domains. Firehouse Subs had 121, with names like flrehousesubs.delivery, an l where the i should be. Jersey Mike’s had 80, among them mlckessejersstey.delivery and jerseymikes-delivery.com. Dave’s Hot Chicken had 67.

Waffle House got w0ffleh0use.delivery, with zeros for the a and the o. Chipotle, Popeyes, Panera Bread, Five Guys, Little Caesars, Tim Hortons and Wawa are on the list as well, some with a single copy, some with a handful. The earliest copy in the research turned up on March 3, 2026.

Almost all of them, 761 of the 820, sit behind that same service that hides their servers. Of the first 255 the researchers found, 251 were bought from the same shop for web addresses, Dynadot. A shop like that is called a registrar.

One server had a live card panel on it, the place where the card details arrive. A second group of 68 domains is tied to a server on Amazon’s cloud, and some of those sites run straight from it, in Frankfurt, with a slightly different script. The researchers found nothing that shows the same people run both.

In cybersecurity, attribution is one of the hardest problems. A kit can be shared or sold. A server address tells you where a machine is rented, not who rents it. What we know for sure is how these sites work.

On November 4, 367 of the 820 domains still served a site.

To bring people to them, the scammers bought Google search ads. The researchers found at least 47 of them between July 7 and October 20, 2026. And they only looked up ads for the sites from their first search, so there were probably more.

The ads ran under 46 separate advertiser accounts with 43 different business names, and those names look unrelated to the chains: construction firms, a watch company, a reptile rescue. How the scammers got hold of those accounts, the researchers do not say. Most ads ran for one to four days, usually starting a few days after the domain was registered. The longest ran for 56 days, the next for 39.

Google publishes a report each year about the bad ads it stops. The one for 2025 came out on April 16, 2026. The company says it blocked or removed more than 8.3 billion ads and shut down 24.9 million accounts. Its systems caught over 99 percent of the ads that broke its rules before they were ever shown, the report says, and 602 million ads had to do with scams. It also says it checks who its advertisers are.

These 47 got through. Some stayed up for weeks.

An advertiser can pay Google to show an ad when someone searches for another company’s name. That search word is called a keyword, and Google’s trademark policy does not restrict using someone else’s brand there. Many of the ads also put the brand name in the headline itself, followed by words like Menu Items or Catering Menu.

The 20 Jimmy John’s ads did not. Their headlines said Sandwich Shop or Order Sandwiches for Delivery, so a trademark complaint from the chain would have found no brand name in the ad to point at.

Google has a second rule that needs no complaint at all. Its policy against misleading ads bans pretending to be another brand or business, in the ad or on the website behind it. It treats that as one of its most serious violations and can suspend the account without warning. These ads sent people to sites that pretended to be the restaurant. They still ran, most of them for a few days only.

The man whose company found all of this knows the ad business from the inside. Rob Leathern, its CEO and co-founder, was VP of Privacy and Security Product at Google and led Business Integrity at Meta, according to its own team page. The company sells tools to detect exactly this kind of clone, and the report ends with an offer to check whether someone is copying your brand.

The trick itself is older than this campaign. On February 24, 2023, the writer Cory Doctorow described searching for a Thai restaurant he liked in Burbank, Kiin Thai. He clicked a sponsored result for a site called kiinthaila.com, built on Wix, while the restaurant’s own website was the third link down. The copy added 15 percent to the prices, passed the order on to the restaurant and billed him twice.

The restaurant called him to cancel and told him to contact his card company to get the charge reversed. That version still produced an order. The 2026 version produces none, shows the restaurant’s live menu instead of a copied one, and goes after your bank code too.

Two months before that post, on December 21, 2022, the FBI had already warned about this. It wrote that criminals were buying search ads with web addresses that look like a known business. Those ads showed up at the very top of the results and looked almost the same as the normal ones. Its advice back then: check the address before you click an ad, type the address of a business yourself instead of searching for it, and use an ad blocker.

The chains in this campaign are American. A fake site that pulls the pages from the original and only swaps the payment box would work the same way for a pizza place in Rotterdam or a delivery service in Berlin.

By November 3, none of the ads the researchers found were still running, and Google’s own page for looking up ads now shows Can’t find ad for them.

Restaurants have one way to spot this early. The fake site has to ask the restaurant’s own server for each page. So a chain that watches for its pages showing up under a strange web address, or for checkouts that never reach its payment company, can catch these sites fast.

What you can do before you pay for food online:

  • → Type the restaurant’s address yourself, use a bookmark, or order through its own app
  • → Look at the domain in the address bar. A secure connection only tells you it is encrypted
  • → A brand name followed by .delivery, -delivery.com or -us.com was the pattern in this campaign
  • → Read the full text from your bank before you type a code anywhere. If the shop or the amount does not match your order, stop
  • → Pay with a credit card where you can, so you can dispute the charge
  • → Use an ad blocker, one of the tips from that 2022 warning
  • → If you typed your card into a site like this, call your bank, block the card, and in the US report it at ic3.gov

item.title: Fake GitHub Security Tools Infected Over 2,000 Windows Machines
item.description:
More than 2,000 Windows machines have been taken over by the security tools their owners cloned from GitHub and built themselves. The people getting hit are cybersecurity professionals, paid to stop exactly this. The fake repositories have been going up for two years, and some are still online today.

The trap works the way these people already work. A researcher needs a scanner, a reverse proxy, a script to clean up the output of another tool. They search GitHub, they find a repository that looks right, they clone it, and they build it. That last step is the one that ends it. The moment they build it, or even only open it, the machine is no longer theirs.

Doctor Web pulled the malware apart on November 5, 2026, and named the loader that runs it all Trojan.Loader.3261. The researchers found the malicious code hidden inside three kinds of project files, and each one fires in a different way.

In a Visual Studio C# project, the trap sits in the .csproj file as a pre-build event. A pre-build event is a command the project runs before the compiler even starts, meant for ordinary things like copying a file or stamping a version number. Here it runs a PowerShell command instead, the second the developer hits build.

In the same project there is a second file, the .suo, that holds another PowerShell command. The .suo lives in a hidden .vs folder that a developer rarely opens and that a file manager hides by default. In October 2023, Zhiniang Peng of Sangfor showed that a crafted .suo file can run code when a Visual Studio solution is simply opened, before anything is compiled at all. Microsoft did not treat that as a vulnerability. It said opening a project from an untrusted source is an insecure operation, and that users should turn on the trust settings to protect themselves.

The third path is for the Python and Go versions of these fake tools. There the malicious code is pushed far off the right edge of the file, behind a long run of whitespace, so a developer scrolling through the source sees a blank line and reads straight past it.

Once any of those three fires, a PowerShell script lands on disk and reaches out. It pulls an encrypted link from the attackers’ own servers and, alongside them, from ordinary places: YouTube, Telegram, Google Docs, GitCode and Pastebin. Traffic to those everyday sites looks like nothing on a corporate network. The decrypted link downloads an archive called Quixo.7z, which unpacks into a folder dressed up to look like a Windows photo component.

Inside that archive sits Microsoft.exe, and this is the program that does the damage. Doctor Web found it at version 1.4.5. It is built with Electron, the same toolkit behind many everyday desktop apps, so on the machine it looks like one more normal program. Then it goes after the defenses, one by one. It turns off Windows Defender, User Account Control, the pop-up warnings, System Restore and the Volume Shadow Copy Service that backups lean on.

The loader goes further. It puts RegAsm.exe and dwm.exe on Defender’s exclusion list, so the code it later hides in them is never scanned. It tries to remove three security products, McAfee, ESET and Malwarebytes. And it rewrites the Windows hosts file so the machine can no longer even reach the websites of antivirus makers. When it is done, the machine has no guard left and no way to call out for a new one.

Getting that code to run without setting off an alarm is a job on its own, and the loader has a trick for each guard. It makes its own process look like a child of explorer.exe, the program behind your desktop, so it passes for something Windows started itself. It flips a setting in the registry to slip past Smart App Control, the check that is meant to block untrusted apps.

Security tools work by hooking into Windows and watching what runs through. So the loader quietly pulls those hooks back out. It reads a clean copy of ntdll.dll, a core Windows file, straight from disk and uses it to undo them. It calls Windows directly, underneath the layer where the watching happens, a move known as Halo’s Gate. And it switches off two parts of Windows, called ETW and AMSI, that would otherwise let a scanner watch what is running. The payloads end up tucked inside trusted programs like RegAsm.exe and dwm.exe.

What it drops is built to pay off in more than one way. The loader installs two separate copies of the AsyncRAT backdoor. They are identical except for the network port each one uses, and the researchers say this could let two operators hold the same machine at once, each through its own port. One infected computer, two operators, neither of them the person who bought it.

Alongside the backdoors comes a clipboard stealer. It watches for a cryptocurrency wallet address being copied and swaps in the attackers’ address, so money meant for one wallet lands in another. On each swap it grabs a screenshot and sends it to a Telegram bot, together with the title of the active window, the username and the machine’s IP address.

The last piece is an information stealer, and what it goes after is exactly what sits on a security professional’s laptop. It checks first whether it is running in a sandbox or a virtual machine. If the coast is clear, it collects browser data, the saved sites and passwords in FileZilla, the MobaXterm.ini file full of saved SSH sessions, Total Commander’s FTP logins, VPN settings, messenger files, gaming accounts and Discord tokens. All of it gets packed up and sent out through the Telegram bot. These are the keys to other people’s networks, held by the people paid to defend them.

The campaign began somewhere else entirely. In the early days the fake repositories were bots and cheats for crypto games, including one built around the Telegram game Catizen, going after people chasing a quick token. For readers without the right setup, some of those repositories even walked them through installing Visual Studio and cloning the project, step by step.

At some point the operators turned toward a richer target and started dressing the same malware up as scanning tools, security testing tools and log analysis scripts. The researchers also found a component that is not finished yet, built to install the loader as a Windows service and re-download it if it is ever removed. Whoever runs this is still building.

These repositories are still out there. Checking the ones in Doctor Web’s published indicators this morning, two days after the report, several were still live. One is advertised as a lightweight script to parse and clean up the output of Fscan, a network scanner with nearly 15,000 stars that security testers rely on. Another lifts its description straight from a genuine open-source tool, so it reads as legitimate at a glance. Two of the nine example repositories now return a 404. The rest were still there.

Researchers have run into this same toolkit before. In June 2025, Trend Micro wrote about a campaign it called Water Curse, with at least 76 GitHub accounts pushing fake penetration-testing tools. It used the very same parts: a pre-build event in a .csproj, an Electron app, a scheduled task that relaunches a Microsoft.exe on a timer, code slipped into RegAsm.exe, and Telegram used the same way to carry the stolen data out.

The overlap runs down to the internal file names. Trend Micro found the same hidden modules in 2025, boot_f, kernel_f and thread_f, and could only guess what some of them did. Doctor Web has now taken the same pieces apart. The file names and the methods line up that closely, but that does not prove the same people are behind both.

In security, working out who did it is one of the hardest problems there is. Tools get shared, sold and copied, and the same tricks can belong to one group or to several using the same playbook. What we can be sure of is how the malware works, not whose hands are on the keyboard.

Hiding code behind a long stretch of whitespace is older still. In February 2025, Kaspersky wrote up GitVenom, hundreds of fake GitHub projects where the Python payload sat behind about 2,000 tab characters. One of the attackers’ wallets took in roughly 5 BTC, about 485,000 dollars at the time.

Handing a security researcher a Visual Studio project with a trap inside is an old idea. In January 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group described a campaign it put down to a government-backed group in North Korea. The attackers made contact, offered to work together on research, and sent over a project with a malicious DLL wired to run through the build events. That is Google’s read on that 2021 case, and nothing here ties it to the GitHub campaign running now.

After that, Microsoft added a trust setting you can switch on, one that makes you approve a project from an untrusted source before it opens. It stays off unless you turn it on yourself. A warning that appears on its own came later, in Visual Studio 2022 version 17.12 from November 2024, and only when the file carries a Mark of the Web, the little tag Windows puts on anything you download. Code pulled straight down with git clone often has no such tag, so no warning shows up.

So the defense comes down to a habit. Before opening a cloned project, look inside the project file itself. In a Visual Studio project, open the .csproj in a plain text editor and check for a pre-build event you did not expect:

1
2
3

<Target Name="PreBuild" BeforeTargets="PreBuildEvent">
  <Exec Command="powershell -enc ..." />
</Target>

A line like that, calling PowerShell or a script before the code even compiles, has no legitimate reason to sit in a tool you cloned minutes ago. Older projects tuck the same command inside a plain <PreBuildEvent> tag, so look for either. Delete the hidden .vs folder before you open the solution, so a planted .suo cannot run. Scroll Python and Go files all the way to the right, past where the text seems to end. And do all of it on a throwaway virtual machine with a clean snapshot, never on the laptop that holds your working keys. Doctor Web published the full list of indicators, the four attacker domains, the IP addresses and the file hashes, in its malware-iocs repository, and its products detect and remove this family.
